extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method (scholars, scientists, and advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for explaining natural phenomena and for inventing, using, and judging scientific hypotheses—distinguishing ultimate vs. derivative laws, limits of explanation, and the proper method of hypothesis-driven deduction and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ultimate and derivative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws are deducible from, and may be resolved into, other and more general ones. Ultimate laws are those which cannot (be so resolved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when seeking explanations: try to resolve derivative laws into more general laws. Recognize that even when a law is resolved into others, ultimate laws must remain; progress consists in reducing derivative into more general laws. (Original wording: 'two kinds of laws, or observed uniformities in nature: ultimate laws, and what may be termed derivative laws.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate laws limited by distinguishable states of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate laws of nature cannot possibly be less numerous than the distinguishable sensations or other feelings of our nature (distinct in quality, not merely degree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to reduce phenomena of fundamentally different qualitative kinds (e.g., colour vs. heat) purely to laws of another kind; any complete explanation will retain a last link corresponding to that qualitative class. Example: attempts to explain white by red laws still require a law of white.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as resolution into causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining scientifically means resolving an observed uniformity which is not a law of causation into the laws of causation from which it results, or resolving a complex law of causation into simpler and more general ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an explanation, check whether the proposed account deductively yields the observed uniformity as resulting from causal laws. Explanations that merely restate observations without causal grounding are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use and character of scientific hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition made (without actual evidence, or on insufficient evidence) in order to deduce conclusions in accordance with known facts; if those conclusions are known truths, the hypothesis may be (or is likely to be) true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are instruments to enable the Deductive Method: they may be invented to provide laws from which consequences are deduced and then verified. Examples: inverse-square law initially suggested as hypothesis; vortices of Descartes as a fictitious hypothesis; vortex/ether hypotheses supposed to obey known laws. Use hypotheses cautiously and for their deductive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility constraint on hypotheses (analogy with known laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses gain plausibility when they ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature; wholly arbitrary hypotheses (agent and law both fictitious) lack such plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that posit either (a) a real agent with a supposed law of action or (b) a fictitious agent whose behaviour follows laws similar to known phenomena. Avoid inventing both a wholly new agent and wholly new laws without analogical support or independent evidence. Anti-pattern: assuming unproven entities solely for explanatory convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three indispensable parts of discovery by the Deductive Method
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the cause of any phenomenon by the Deductive Method the process must consist of three parts: induction (to ascertain laws of the causes), ratiocination (to compute from those laws how the causes will operate in particular combinations), and verification (by comparing calculated effect with the actual phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the three parts can be dispensed with. Evaluate proposed explanations by checking that (1) inductive grounds for the laws are present, (2) correct deductive reasoning is used to derive consequences, and (3) empirical verification has been performed. Example: Newton's derivation/verification of gravitation involved all three steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate vs illegitimate hypotheses (need for evidence of assumed entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defect of some hypotheses lies not in attempting to reduce phenomena, but in assuming the existence of entities (or the law of their operation) without proof, relying only on the facility they afford for explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a hypothesis, demand independent evidence for any postulated entity or for the law by which it operates, not merely the explanatory convenience. Example: theories of light invoking a vibrating fluid (ether) were defective when the fluid's existence and motion were unproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses invented to enable earlier deduction but require later verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are invented to enable the Deductive Method to be earlier applied to phenomena; they allow deduction of consequences that can later be checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as provisional tools: they are acceptable as long as they produce testable consequences and are subjected to verification. Hypotheses failing to yield verifiable consequences (or contradicted by them) should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of attempting general unifying explanations (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to resolve many observed modes of a phenomenon into one kind of cause (e.g., all motion produced by the same kind of cause) are legitimate; successes in physics (e.g., uniting terrestrial fall and planetary motion under gravitation) justify such attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage search for unifying, more general laws, particularly where the experienced phenomenon is 'the same in every respect but degree' (e.g., motion). But maintain the earlier cautions about evidence and avoid conflating qualitatively distinct phenomena without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of different senses of explanation and their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing on what conditions a phenomenon depends is not the same as showing what the thing is; discovering conditions may not give insight into the phenomenon's nature, but is nevertheless a legitimate scientific aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ontological accounts ('what a thing is') and causal/conditional accounts ('what it depends on'). Value causal accounts even if they do not dissolve the qualitative character of phenomena (e.g., colour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful explanatory domains (where reduction often works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science has been most successful in explaining phenomena by resolving their laws into more general ones chiefly in cases of propagation through space (notably motion), where differences are largely differences of degree rather than kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing domains to pursue unification, prioritize phenomena that present as continuous/differing in degree (e.g., motions, vibrations) because reduction to general laws is often more attainable there; historical examples include gravitation, unification of electricity and magnetism, fluid mechanics accounts of diverse motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the dogmatic interdict against reduction of 'primordial' properties
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not unphilosophical to attempt to discover conditions of phenomena considered 'primordial' (e.g., specific colours); the real objection is to assuming unproved entities rather than the attempt itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept as a methodological rule that certain classes of properties are unexplainable. Investigative attempts are legitimate, provided any introduced hypotheses or entities are tested and evidence for them is sought.
